tldr: REALM-Bench introduces a benchmark suite of 14 planning and scheduling problems designed to evaluate multi-agent systems under dynamic, real-world conditions with disruptions, scalability, and multi-agent coordination requirements.
contributions: 14 benchmark problems spanning 10 P-series (general planning) and 4 J-series (Job-Shop Scheduling Problem) variants, progressing from static single-agent tasks to dynamic multi-agent coordination under severe disruptions
Standardized evaluation metrics combining planning quality (goal satisfaction, solution completeness) and planning optimality (makespan minimization, resource efficiency)
Integration support for five major LLM-agent frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Swarm, ALAS) and six+ LLM families
Open-source release with public leaderboards, automated result aggregation, and extensibility for community contributions
methods: The authors designed 14 benchmark scenarios across five difficulty tiers, each scalable along three dimensions: number of parallel planning threads, complexity of inter-dependencies, and frequency of unexpected disruptions. Problems include campus navigation (P1), campus tour scheduling (P2), urban ridesharing (P3/P4), wedding reunion logistics (P5), Thanksgiving dinner planning (P6/P9 with disruptions), disaster relief logistics (P7/P8), and global supply chain for data center GPU deployment (P10). The JSSP problems range from basic sequential (J1) to large-scale with stochastic delays and material disruptions (J4). Each problem supports small-to-large instance scaling while maintaining tractability for evaluation.
results: The paper describes 15 comparison methods tested including Random, LPT, SPT, STPT, MPSR, DRL-Liu, GP, GEP, LSO, SPT/TWKR, DRL-Chen, DRL-Zhang, and baseline implementations using GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, DeepSeek-R1, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Swarm. A key finding is that current LLM-based systems fail to leverage early disruption notices—for example, when a flight delay is communicated at 10 AM for a 1 PM arrival, existing LLM solutions do not adapt until 1 PM, missing the window for earlier intervention. The results section was truncated in the provided text, so detailed numerical results are not available.
limitations: LLMs are inherently stateless, making it difficult for them to track previous scheduling events and adapt plans in real-time
Current LLM-based systems fail to react proactively to early disruption notifications, only responding at originally scheduled times
Existing benchmarks evaluated lacked dynamic complexity, transaction properties, and long-lived episode support—gaps this benchmark addresses but which remain challenges for system designers
Dynamic disruptions such as machine breakdowns, power outages, and material shortages require sophisticated reactive planning that current systems struggle with
